title: Voyager 1’s messages take almost a full day to reach us
body: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 flew past Jupiter and Saturn and simply kept going. It is now more than 170 times farther from the Sun than Earth is, making it the most distant human-made object, and its radio signals, travelling at the speed of light, need roughly 23 to 24 hours to arrive. It is projected to reach one full light-day from Earth in November 2026. NASA still listens for its faint whisper with giant 70-metre dishes.

slides.question: In Earth–Sun distances (AU), how far out did Voyager 1 cross the heliopause into interstellar space?
slides.explanation: 121 AU, four times Neptune’s distance, on 25 August 2012. By October 2026 Voyager 1 was 172.5 AU from Earth, still moving outward at about 61,000 km/h.

slides.heading: Earliest first
items: Voyager 1 flies past Jupiter and Saturn
slides.explanation: Voyager 2 left first; Voyager 1 followed 16 days later, on 5 September 1977, took a faster route past Jupiter and Saturn, and crossed the heliopause in 2012.

slides.heading: Launched second
slides.text: Despite its name, Voyager 1 left Earth 16 days after its twin, Voyager 2, on 5 September 1977. A faster route soon put it in the lead.

slides.heading: Into interstellar space
slides.text: On 25 August 2012 it crossed the heliopause, where the Sun’s wind gives way to the gas between stars, the first spacecraft ever to do so.

slides.heading: Running on plutonium
slides.text: Its nuclear generators made about 470 watts at launch. Output keeps falling, so instruments are being switched off, but it may keep working into the 2030s.
